Look for the math

A complex number is a point (x, y) of the plane, written x + yi. Adding is easy; multiplying turns out to be turning and stretching.

Adding and multiplying

Numbers add componentwise, which is the parallelogram rule for arrows: (x1, y1) + (x2, y2) = (x1 + x2, y1 + y2). The product is (x1x2 − y1y2, x1y2 + x2y1). Fix the absolute values of both numbers and drag the angles: the product always stays on one circle, of radius |A|·|B|, because moduli multiply and arguments add. The logic test confirmed this for every board position tried.

Easy multipliers

A real factor only stretches (the argument is unchanged); multiplying by a number on the imaginary axis turns by 90° counter-clockwise; multiplying by −1 reflects in the origin. The conjugate reflects in the real axis, so conjugating twice gives the number back.

The real and complex products

The real product x1x2 + y1y2 is always on the real axis and is zero exactly when the arrows are perpendicular: it is the dot product. The complex product is always on the imaginary axis and is zero exactly when A, B and the origin are in a line. A small catch: the page's formula (z1 Conj(z2) − Conj(z1) z2)/2 gives (y1x2 − x1y2)i, while the applet draws (x1y2 − x2y1)i, the opposite sign. This port follows the applet; the two agree about where it is zero.

Fix the angle, then slide A along its line through the origin while showing the common product: where does it go?
